source: Spamann & Klöhn (2016) Justice is less blind, and less legalistic, than we thought: evidence from an experiment with real judges
finding: US federal judges decided a real-style appeal. A weak precedent had no detectable effect on outcomes. A legally irrelevant defendant trait had a large effect.
numbers: N=32 judges, about 55 minutes each, 2x2 between-subject design. Affirmance 87% (13/15) for the unsympathetic defendant vs 41% (7/17) for the sympathetic one; gap 45 points, Boschloo p<.01. Precedent: 64% (9/14) vs 61% (11/18), almost identical.
limits: Small N. Precedents were deliberately weak. Authors say results do not show that law does not matter; a strong precedent might bind. Judges' written reasons never mentioned the defendant trait.
agent_relevance: Stated reasons that cite a precedent are not proof the precedent drove the answer. The agent should test which facts actually move the answer (mutate inputs) and not trust its own cited analogy.

source: Spamann & Klöhn (2016) Justice is less blind, and less legalistic, than we thought: evidence from an experiment with real judges
finding: Legal experts mispredicted how much precedent matters. Law professors expected precedent to beat irrelevant defendant traits; the data pointed the other way.
numbers: Survey of 102 law professors: 66 said the precedent effect would be stronger, 13 said the defendant effect. Informative comparison cell (19 observations): 75% vs 39% = 36 points, p<0.11, Bayes factor 8.7 for defendant over precedent. Posterior odds 13/89 x 8.7 = 1.27.
limits: Not significant at the conventional level. Bayes factor depends on flat priors. Tiny N.
agent_relevance: Expert intuition about what drives analogy-based judgement is poor. Do not use expert opinion as the check that a precedent was applied; use a counterfactual test.

source: Spamann & Klöhn (2016) Justice is less blind, and less legalistic, than we thought: evidence from an experiment with real judges
finding: Conflict between sympathetic facts and precedent did not significantly slow judges.
numbers: Judges spent about 2 minutes more on legal materials when defendant trait and precedent conflicted; the difference was about 1 SD, not significant.
limits: Underpowered.
agent_relevance: Time spent is a weak signal of an impasse in analogical choice.

source: Liu, Klöhn & Spamann (2019/2021) Precedent and Chinese judges: an experiment
finding: Near-replication of the Spamann-Klöhn design in China. A strong defendant-friendly precedent did move judges, although Chinese judges may not cite precedent and most say it matters little.
numbers: N=48 Chinese judges. Affirmance 86% (Sainovic precedent) and 82% (Vasiljevic) vs 40% under the strongly favourable Besic precedent, about 44 points lower. Fisher exact p = 0.020 (all three), 0.015 and 0.039 (pairwise).
limits: Small N, three precedents, a fictitious case built on an ICTY case. Weak precedents again did little (86% vs 82%); only the strong one changed outcomes. Same unsympathetic-defendant gap: 23 points, p<.10.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: strength of the precedent matters. The agent should weight analogies by how closely the precedent's facts and holding match, and not treat any cited case as equal.

source: Liu, Klöhn & Spamann (2019/2021) Precedent and Chinese judges: an experiment
finding: Judges used precedent in process but hid it in writing. They read precedents first and longer than statutes, but few cited them.
numbers: Precedent read 13% of total time (2.93 min) vs statute 4% (0.81 min), p<1%. 68% consulted precedent before statute. Only 29% mentioned precedent in written reasons. Recruitment: one session yielded only 24 completers; in another 19 volunteered and 14 completed.
limits: Volunteer, self-selected judges. Chinese setting limits generalisation.
agent_relevance: Written rationale and actual use diverge. G2 fits: check behaviour, not the stated reason.

source: Chen & Li (2018) The foundations of judicial diffusion in China: evidence from an experiment
finding: Citing a case from a sister court shifted how Chinese judges read a vague permissive legal standard. It did not shorten sentences. Law students were moved about as much as judges.
numbers: Abstract states a 'substantial and statistically significant effect'. Sample sizes and effect sizes were not on the page I opened.
limits: Abstract page only; numbers not read. Effect on interpretation but not on sentence length: precedent pulls on standards more than on discretionary quantities.
agent_relevance: Analogy anchors the reading of vague standards more than numeric outputs. Expect the most help where a standard is open-textured.

source: Braman & Nelson (2007) Mechanism of motivated reasoning? Analogical perception in discrimination disputes
finding: Attitudes change how similar a precedent looks to the target case. People call a source case analogous when its outcome fits their policy view.
numbers: Two experiments: undergraduates (Study 1); undergraduates and law students (Study 2). Effect strongest when cases were moderately similar on objective dimensions. No sample sizes or effect sizes on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only. The note that legal training did not reduce the motivated effect came from a summary of that page and is not verified against the paper. Vignette study, not real judges.
agent_relevance: Key mechanism: similarity is not fixed, it is shaped by the wanted outcome. Score similarity on pre-listed features before seeing which outcome helps (hide the outcome while matching), and take extra care with moderately similar cases.

source: Spellman & Schauer (2012) Legal reasoning, in Oxford Handbook of Thinking and Reasoning
finding: Review says there are no data that lawyers or judges are better analogical reasoners in general. Their edge looks content-based (legal knowledge), not process-based.
numbers: Cites Lehman, Lempert & Nisbett (1988): first-year law students beat medical and graduate students on verbal reasoning, but after three years their gain was not significant while others improved more.
quote: there are no data to support that judges' ability to use analogies transcends the domains in which they normally operate.
limits: Secondary report of a 1988 study; I did not open the original. Absence of data is not evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Legal analogy skill is knowledge of which relations matter. Give the agent the doctrine's element list as the feature set; do not hope a generic reasoner finds the right similarity.

source: Spellman & Schauer (2012) Legal reasoning, in Oxford Handbook of Thinking and Reasoning
finding: Rival to the Realist view: judges choose analogies because of prior knowledge and how the question is framed, not only because of a wanted outcome. Legal categories are relational, and relations count more than attributes in analogy.
numbers: Review states relations are generally more important than attributes for analogical retrieval; training on which relations matter helps analogical reminding. Cites Holyoak & Koh (1987) on surface vs structural similarity.
limits: Argument plus secondary citations; no new numbers in the section I read.
agent_relevance: Retrieve precedents by relation structure (who did what to whom, which elements are met), not topic words. See the AALawyer retrieval failure in b22.

source: Schauer & Spellman (2017) Analogy, expertise, and experience, U Chicago Law Review 84:249
finding: Analogy begins with a perceived similarity, but that perception depends on the reasoner's knowledge, training and experience. It is neither pure rule-making nor disguised lawmaking.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers.
limits: Abstract page only. Theory paper.
agent_relevance: Similarity judgement is expertise-dependent, so the agent's similarity step should use a domain feature set and be checked against held-out labelled pairs (G3).

source: Marchant, Robinson, Anderson & Schadewald (1993) The use of analogy in legal argument: problem similarity, precedent, and expertise
finding: Tax-case studies: experts and novices relied on the structurally matched analog and ignored the surface analog once pragmatic concerns were held constant; pragmatic goals override similarity constraints.
numbers: From a search-engine summary only: Study 1 had 63 graduate students and 38 professionals; Study 2 had 128 professionals and 146 students. A companion 1991 study found facilitating treatments reduced transfer for experts and raised it for novices.
limits: NOT opened. The abstract page said no abstract and full text is paywalled. Second-hand and unverified.
agent_relevance: If true, expose structure (elements) and purpose rather than surface description.

source: Alexander (1996) Bad beginnings, U Penn Law Review
finding: Skeptic position: analogical reasoning in law adds nothing beyond rules or principles. It attacks Sunstein and others. Schauer (Playing by the Rules, 1991) is named as an earlier critic.
numbers: None; theory.
limits: NOT opened: PDF blocked (403). Only a search snippet seen.
agent_relevance: Rival theory: analogy is a rule or principle in disguise. Test it: write the stated holding as an explicit rule and see whether it reproduces the analogy's verdict.

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray & Ashley (2026) Thinking longer, not always smarter: evaluating LLM capabilities in hierarchical legal reasoning
finding: CATO-style factor framework with a symbolic solver for ground truth. Models are perfect at spotting factual distinctions between the current case and a precedent, but fall away as steps are chained.
numbers: n=253 instances per task. Task 1 (find distinctions): 100% for every model. Task 2 (argumentative role of distinctions): 64.82% to 92.09%. Task 3 (all significant distinctions, integrated): 11.46% to 33.99%, most under 25%.
limits: Synthetic factor-based problems from the CATO trade-secret domain, not free text. Five reasoning models plus one non-thinking Qwen.
agent_relevance: Single steps of analogy and distinction are cheap; composing them is where models fail. Split into code-checked steps and let code do the combination.

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray & Ashley (2026) Thinking longer, not always smarter: evaluating LLM capabilities in hierarchical legal reasoning
finding: Thinking mode helps a lot on the middle task. Longer thinking is not a sign of being right.
numbers: Qwen3 thinking 78.66% vs non-thinking 30.04% on Task 2 (2.6x); Task 3 non-thinking 0.00% vs thinking 33.99%. gpt-5 used 4,456 tokens on wrong Task 2 answers vs 3,081 on right ones (+45%).
limits: Table columns in the PDF text were garbled, so only numbers quoted in running text are used. Averages, no per-item test.
agent_relevance: Token count signals difficulty, not correctness. Use heavy token spend as a trigger to decompose or check (G1 signal), never as a confidence cue.

source: Zhang, Savelka & Ashley (2025) Do LLMs truly 'understand' when a precedent is overruled?
finding: Models struggle to name which precedent a Supreme Court case overruled.
numbers: 236 US Supreme Court case pairs. Task 1 open identification: Gemini-Pro 73.31% (173/236), GPT-5 71.19%, Gemini-Flash 33.47%, Qwen3 2.12%. Task 2 closed verification: GPT-5 75.42% vs Gemini-Pro 42.37% (131 abstentions). Task 3 temporal impossibility: GPT-5 and Gemini-Pro 100%.
limits: Long-context benchmark. Grader was GPT-4o, 98% consistent with human experts on a 10% sample. Snapshot of 2025 models.
agent_relevance: An analogy is useless if the precedent is no longer good law. Add a code-side validity check on each retrieved case before reasoning from it.

source: Zhang, Savelka & Ashley (2025) Do LLMs truly 'understand' when a precedent is overruled?
finding: Era sensitivity: accuracy on older cases is far below recent ones, a temporal bias.
limits: Small earliest-era cell (about 17 cases). Authors say models lean on shallow logical heuristics.
agent_relevance: Analogy quality depends on training coverage of the era or domain. Retrieve the text instead of recalling from memory.

source: Fan et al. (2025/2026) Legal rule induction: towards generalizable principle discovery from analogous judicial precedents
finding: Task: induce the shared rule from a set of analogous cases. Frontier LLMs over-generalise and hallucinate; small models tuned on the data catch up.
numbers: 5,121 case sets (38,088 Chinese court cases), 216 expert-annotated test sets. Direct Mic-F1 from the text: Gemini-2.5-Flash 60.51%, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 66.67%. LoRA Ministral-8B: Mic-F1 73.18%, Mac-F1 70.73%; Llama-3.2-3B from 19.21% to 70.96%. Abstract claims over 76% F1 gains for 3B-8B tuned models.
limits: Chinese criminal law only. Training labels are silver, from DeepSeek-R1. Long chain-of-thought effects were mixed: Gemini Mic-F1 +2.45%, Claude Mic-F1 -0.89%.
agent_relevance: Extracting the rule linking similar cases is a distinct, checkable step. Keep the induced rule and test it on held-out cases.

source: Fan et al. (2025/2026) Legal rule induction
finding: Implicit rules are recalled far less often than explicit ones. Chain-of-thought moves the precision-recall balance without a clear net gain.
numbers: In the direct-induction table, explicit-rule recall was above implicit-rule recall in every row I could read, for example 73.00 vs 37.77. Long-CoT raised Gemini-2.5-Flash precision by 9.08 points while lowering recall.
limits: Table rows are garbled in text extraction, so I do not attribute rows to models. Chinese benchmark.
agent_relevance: Implicit norms are the hard part of what makes a case like this one. Add an explicit step asking what rule would justify both the precedent and the present case.

source: Han et al. (2025) CourtReasoner: can LLM agents reason like judges?
finding: Deep-research agents writing judicial reasoning from precedent often give invalid arguments and irrelevant citations.
numbers: Abstract: more than 60% of frontier-model outputs had invalid arguments and more than 53% had irrelevant citations. Human scores (0-4): GPT-4o Deep Research default citation relevance 3.33, constraint extraction 2.96, argument validity 3.08. 292 expert-annotated meta-evaluation examples.
limits: Inter-annotator agreement 66.7% to 92.3% by cell. Cells of 5 to 50 examples. Deep-research agents, not plain models.
agent_relevance: Cited authority must be checked for relevance in code or by a separate pass. Fluent citations are not evidence of fit.

source: Han et al. (2025) CourtReasoner
finding: Perturbation test: removing the most important fact lowers quality. Arguing the losing side is harder than arguing the winning side.
numbers: Gemini Deep Research citation relevance 2.07 with the most important fact deleted, 2.28 second-most, 2.80 least important (5 examples). GPT-4o Deep Research opposite-side citation relevance 2.42 vs 3.33 default. Open-RAG, restricted to case law, scored 3.00 on argument validity by default and had no 0 or 1 ratings.
limits: Cells of 10 to 30 outputs. No significance tests reported.
agent_relevance: Fact-deletion is a cheap held-out check (G3). Drop the key fact and see whether answer and citation change; if not, the analogy was not being used.

source: Han et al. (2025) CourtReasoner
finding: LLM graders of legal reasoning are uneven. Claude aligned best with experts; some graders correlate near zero or negatively on retrieval-augmented outputs.
numbers: Spearman up to 75 (constraint extraction) and 81 (argument validity) for Claude grading GPT-4o opposite-side outputs. Qwen2.5-72B correlations drop to zero or negative on Open-RAG and open-deep-research outputs. Gemini graders do well on their own outputs only.
limits: Spearman values on small subsets. Graders were given the rubric.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: a model judge of analogy quality is unreliable and favours its own family. Use code checks where possible.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Mitigating legal hallucinations via symbolic constraints and analogical precedents (AALawyer)
finding: Dense retrieval confuses similar-sounding but legally different provisions (semantic drift). Adding analogical precedent retrieval plus a closed-set constraint on article labels cuts hallucination.
numbers: Versus DeepSeek-7B base: hallucination risk down 37.6%, professionalism +13.4%, informativeness +41.9%, explainability +43.4%, average +34.1%. Symbolic constrained retrieval: 0.93 average accuracy, 59% lower hallucination risk. Automated metrics correlate with human experts, Pearson 0.9074.
limits: Chinese criminal law; own benchmark and own metric; 7B base model.
agent_relevance: A crowbar-beating example shows word overlap with a wrong article beating the abstract legal concept. Retrieve on elements and relations; constrain output to a closed list (code checks membership).

source: Demir & Canbaz (2026) Validate your authority: benchmarking LLMs on multi-label precedent treatment classification
finding: Classifying how later courts treated a precedent (followed, distinguished, criticised, overruled) is hard even for 2026 models, and plain accuracy hides serious errors.
numbers: 239 expert-annotated citations. Gemini 2.5 Flash best on the high-level schema, accuracy 0.7908; GPT-5-mini best on the fine-grained schema, 0.6771. Proposes Average Severity Error to weight serious confusions more.
limits: Small dataset. Labels are partly subjective (court criticising vs questioning a precedent). I read abstract, results and discussion, not appendices.
agent_relevance: Whether a precedent was followed or distinguished is subjective at the boundary. Use severity-weighted scoring when analogy errors have unequal costs.

source: Spellman & Schauer (2012) Legal reasoning
finding: Judges fall for standard reasoning biases (anchoring, hindsight) even with legal framing, but those tasks were not real legal tasks.
numbers: Cites Guthrie, Rachlinski & Wistrich (2001); no numbers in the chapter text I read.
limits: Secondary citation; original not opened. Spamann-Klöhn (b01) is the closer real-task evidence.
agent_relevance: Expect the agent's analogy choice to share the anchoring and motivated-similarity drift of human experts. Add held-out checks.

source: Spamann & Klöhn (2016) Justice is less blind
finding: Competing explanation for the precedent null: judges follow strong authority when it exists, and a weak precedent is easy to dismiss. Authors say the null is not evidence that law does not matter.
numbers: Defendant-trait effect 45 points versus about 0 for precedent. Only 19 of 32 observations are informative on relative size.
limits: Authors' interpretation. The China follow-up (b04) supports it: only the strong precedent moved outcomes.
agent_relevance: Weak vs strong analogy: record an explicit strength grade and abstain from firm conclusions on weak analogies.
